author: Bernard, Besenval & Marquis
name_in_asr: Top-é Rustam / Top-e Rustam; Navasanghārāma, Nawbahār (Navavihāra)
asr_identification: Top-e Rustam, the great stupa outside the walls in the SW suburb of Balkh, Balkh province, Afghanistan, as the stupa Xuanzang names with the Navasaṃghārāma (after Foucher)
evidence: Bernard restates Foucher's excavation of Top-e Rustam: the primary stupa had lost nearly all its fired-brick facing over a core of pisé and mud brick, with no decoration beyond a few fired-brick pilasters, and was later coarsely restored with a thick mud-brick casing, the state Xuanzang would have seen in 630. Foucher's dimensions (n. 82): base 54 m square, drum 43 m in diameter (47 m with the casing), 9 m preserved, total height estimated at 60 m; a single Vasudeva coin in the debris. Bernard accepts a Great Kushan construction but rejects Foucher's blaming of the damage on the Hephthalites: the abandonment may reflect a long eclipse of Buddhism or simple neglect and robbing of bricks, and need not be dated with the dismantling at Tepe Zargaran.
quote: Top-é Rustam « la butte de Rostam », dont il soupçonnait avec raison qu’elle cachait les ruines d’un stupa de grandes dimensions que le pèlerin chinois mentionne dans le faubourg sud-ouest de la ville en liaison avec le fameux Navasangharama…c’est ce second état qu’aurait vu Hiuen-tsang en 630
note: Agrees with the study and Mizutani (stupa probably Top-i-Rustam, medium); no new excavation, it restates Foucher. It adds his dimensions: an estimated 60 m height is of the order of the text's 高二百餘尺 (c. 59 m at a Tang chi of c. 29.5 cm; my reckoning, not the authors'). Nothing names the stupa and the monastery is still not found, so the rating stays medium. Date discrepancy: Bernard has Foucher's dig in spring 1925, Besenval (p. 1176) in 1924, as does Foucher himself in the study's note (28 Jan–14 May 1924).

author: Bernard, Besenval & Marquis
asr_identification: the Buddhist temple Nawbahār at Balkh (Bactres), Afghanistan
evidence: Arabic and Persian sources on the Nawbahār after Xuanzang: in 654 Tarkhun Nizak, Hephthalite prince of Badghis, reproached Barmak, the official in charge of the Nawbahār and ancestor of the Barmakids, for converting to Islam, took Balkh and killed him and his sons (after Markwart, Ghirshman); in 705 another Nizak came to pray at the Nawbahār (Ṭabarī II, 1205); Yāqūt says the wind carried the silk of the banner on its dome to Termez, 12 farsakh (60 km) away (n. 67); the Ḥudūd al-ʿĀlam (982) says the Nawbahār, with its paintings, is in ruins (n. 93).
quote: reproche à Barmak, le dignitaire responsable du temple bouddhique de Nawbahār, ancêtre de la fameuse famille des Barmécides…vient prier au Nawbahār pour le succès de son entreprise
note: Agrees: the Nawbahār was a working Buddhist temple at Balkh into the early 8th century and a ruin with paintings in 982, which ties Xuanzang's Navasaṃghārāma to the Nawbahār of the Islamic sources (the study's 'secure by name'). The texts give no position within Balkh; they add nothing to the Top-i-Rustam question.

author: Bernard, Besenval & Marquis
asr_identification: a Kushan stupa in the Tepe Zargaran quarter in the S of the walled city of Balkh, probably inside the rampart
evidence: Excavated 2004 (Creissen): a stupa platform 6 m square faced with dressed limestone, Attic-based pilasters like those of Surkh Kotal; the plundered relic receptacle held a bronze of Soter Megas, so a foundation under the early Kushans; earlier than Top-e Rustam and the other suburban stupas (n. 54). Ten phases in up to 6 m of debris: phases II–III abandonment and burial to the top of the platform, IV an open enclosure over the levelled drum, VI a wall and floors with Kushano-Sasanian and Hephthalite pottery; the cult building had ceased to exist long before. Stones from Buddhist buildings (one capital with a seated Buddha in acanthus) were reused in the hydraulic works of site 6, 400 m away; Bernard dates this dismantling to the Sasanian/Kushano-Sasanian period and infers from Xuanzang (100 monasteries, 3,000 monks, a 20-li circuit 'faiblement peuplé') that the monuments of 630 had been repaired after earlier destruction.
quote: Une chose paraît sûre, c’est qu’à cette date l’édifice de culte a cessé d’exister depuis un certain temps…lorsque Hiuen-tsang visite Bactres en 630, il fait état de 100 couvents habités par 3 000 moines appartenant au Petit Véhicule
note: Agrees with the identification (Balkh, high); adds the first stratified Buddhist monument inside the city, but one abandoned and buried well before 630, so not among the buildings Xuanzang saw. Bernard reads Xuanzang's flourishing Buddhist Balkh as evidence of restoration after Sasanian-period destruction. No change.

author: Bernard, Besenval & Marquis
asr_identification: the rampart of Balkh, its NE section
evidence: 2005 trench (Mongne) 32 × 3 × 5 m across the NE rampart, plus about ten small soundings: at least four building phases (M.I a wall of 35 × 35 cm square bricks; M.II c. 5 m thick, 11 m preserved, with towers; M.III with an inner gallery divided into compartments, a vaulted postern with a bastion and true arrow slits, and fragments of wall painting; M.IV a steep pisé casing and filling of the gallery); no coins and very little pottery, so no absolute date. Le Berre & Schlumberger (1964) dated this NE extension of the city, first confined to the acropolis and then enlarged southward, to the Great Kushans, the 4th–early 5th c. or the mid-5th c. (n. 42). Bernard takes Xuanzang's 20 li as a wall c. 10 km long.
quote: Ce sont, en effet, désormais au moins quatre phases d’aménagement qu’il faut distinguer pour cette partie des murs des fortifications de Bactres…il nous est encore impossible de mettre une chronologie absolue en parallèle à la chronologie relative
note: Bears on the walled city of 630, which the study (after Foucher) places in the Bālā-Hisār: the town wall was in use, rebuilt several times, in the centuries before Xuanzang, but this section is undated. My inference, not the authors': a 20-li (c. 10 km) circuit fits the outer town wall rather than the Bālā-Hisār enclosure alone; Bernard does not say which wall Xuanzang measured. Identification unchanged.

author: Jokura et al.
name_in_asr: アク・ベシム遺跡; ラバト (Rabat, Second Shahristan); シャフリスタン; 唐砕葉城
asr_identification: Ak-Beshim, Chu valley, Kyrgyzstan: the Rabat as the probable Tang Suiye fort; the walled Shahristan (W half of the site) occupied from the 5th c.
evidence: Processing (Aug. 2017) of the 2015 finds. Pottery: 170 sherds from the lower floors of Stratum I in the Shahristan (Tokyo National Research Institute for Cultural Properties trench, 30 × 20 m, c. 100 m N of the S gate, across the main N–S street) compared with Rabat Strata II–III; Shahristan upper Stratum I is Karakhanid (10th c. by five radiocarbon dates of 2012); Rabat Stratum III = Shahristan upper Stratum I, so Rabat II–III are Karakhanid or later. The Shahristan's use is thought to go back to the 5th century. Roof tiles: 62 numbered tiles from Rabat Trench 1 (Stratum IV, by the E wall of the central enclosure) and surface collection (central, canal and Buddhist-temple grids), 3D-scanned; flat tiles made of clay coils on a cloth-covered collapsible mould, some techniques possibly of Chinese origin; joins and identical fabric show a very narrow date range, i.e. the Rabat was built and used within a short span of the Tang period. Final dating of Stratum IV deferred to the final report.
quote: 唐砕葉城の可能性が考えられるラバト中枢部の発掘調査…その利用は 5 世紀にまで遡ると考えられている…この点は、ラバトの造営と利用が唐代の極めて限られた時間幅の中におさまることを意味する。
note: Agrees with the study (Ak-Beshim = Suyab, high) and with Jokura et al. 2017: the tiled Rabat is a short-lived Tang building, so the Tang fort (after 679) is in Shahristan 2, and the town of 630 is the walled Shahristan 1, whose occupation is put back to the 5th c. (cited, not shown here). Adds tile technology, not new location evidence; no change to the rating.

author: Stančo et al.
name_in_asr: Iron Gate of Darband; Darband wall
asr_identification: the Darband (Derbent) wall at Darband village, upper Sherabad Darya, Baysun district, Surkhandarya, Uzbekistan, 'in the vicinity of the famous Iron Gate'
evidence: Czech-Uzbek season 2019: systematic metal-detector survey of the Darband wall (256 man-hours, 629 finds incl. 365 coins and 53 arrowheads; c. 300 diagnostic sherds collected) and cleaning of a section exposed by the new highway at the N end of the wall's central part: 22 units, four walls (the earliest of stone on a pakhsa substructure on gypsum subsoil, a second stone wall perhaps its proteichisma, a third of mud brick); no datable material, radiocarbon pending. The authors frame the wall as evidence for Greek and Yuezhi/Kushan military control; nearby Daganajam Tepa and Mirzali are Hellenistic only. They refer to the French-Uzbek excavations of the wall (Rapin, Khasanov & Rakhmanov 2022, 'from Alexander the Great to the 19th century').
quote: the Czech-Uzbek team aimed to explore the hitherto detected sites in the Bactro-Sogdian borderlands (in the vicinity of the famous Iron Gate of Darband)…including four walls with the earliest phase of a stone wall, which is the best preserved one, being constructed upon a pakhsa substructure
note: Differs in usage only: the study's Iron Gate is the Buzgala defile W of Derbent (secure); this report applies 'Iron Gate of Darband' to the area of the Darband wall at Derbent village, an older barrier wall across the valley, and reports no 7th-c. evidence. It does not test Xuanzang's site or move it; rapin2022_irongates_wall, which covers the wall's later phases, is the item to code for that. No change.
